questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the ___________.
questions.examiner_comment: The question was generally attempted well by the majority of the candidates; however, some candidates selected option (b) 'President' instead of the correct answer (a) 'Lok Sabha'. This response suggests a potential confusion between the concepts of individual and collective responsibility. A few candidates also seemed uncertain about the responsibility of ministers, while others chose the Prime Minister, indicating a partial understanding of the subject.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Bring clarity in the concept of individual and collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers and the Prime Minister. Focus on the fact that in collective responsibility Prime Minister is a part of the Council of Ministers to help students gain full credit in framing the responses.
questions.common_error: Confusion between individual responsibility (to President) and collective responsibility (to Lok Sabha)

By providing a comprehensive understanding of the reasons for adjournment and addressing common misconceptions, students will develop a more nuanced and accurate perspective on parliamentary procedures.
questions.common_error: Assumption that Adjournment Motion could lead to dissolution of Lok Sabha

questions.scheme_text: Leader of the cabinet. / Power to allocate portfolio and /to reshuffle the Council of Ministers. / Power to select /and dismiss Ministers. / Direct and coordinate policies / Resignation of the Prime Minister means the resignation of the ministry. / Formation of the cabinet / Ex officio Chairman of Council of Ministers. / Link between the Cabinet and the President/coordinates with different departments/ Presides over the meeting of the Cabinet./ He is the pivot around which the cabinet revolves, or real head or Keystone of the Cabinet./ He decides the agenda of the Cabinet meeting. questions.model_answer: Two powers of the Prime Minister with reference to the Cabinet are that he is its leader and decides the agenda of its meetings, and that he has the power to allocate portfolios among ministers and to reshuffle the Council of Ministers.

questions.teacher_suggestion: Prepare a classification chart to teach candidates a clear overview of the key differences between the powers and functions of the Prime Minister with reference to the President, the Cabinet, the Lok Sabha, etc., to prevent overlapping of answers.

questions.subject: history_civics

questions.scheme_text: Prayer / Protest / Petition or 3Ps or methods of political mendicancy./ Prepare memorandums / Give speeches / Send deputations or delegations to Britain /Hold meetings/distribution of pamphlets and leaflets/appeals/constitutional methods/passing resolutions/Made use of the press, newspapers, and journals./criticised government policies./ through constitutional methods./ peaceful propaganda/ held discussions/ held processions/. United public opinion/ A British Committee of the JNC was set up in London/ Published a weekly journal 'India' to present India's case before the British Public. (Any two)
questions.model_answer: Two methods an Early Nationalist leader would follow are sending deputations or delegations to Britain to place India's case before the British public, and using the press — newspapers and journals — to criticise government policies through peaceful, constitutional means.
questions.examiner_comment: Several candidates answered this question appropriately; however, few candidates mixed up the categories of powers and functions and gave diverse responses.
questions.teacher_suggestion: To teach the methods used by early nationalists, use approaches such as historical case studies, document analysis, interactive timelines, and debates to help students understand their strategies and contributions to the nationalist movement.

questions.model_answer: Two factors that led to the formation of the Muslim League were the British policy of divide and rule, and the relative backwardness of the Muslim community in education, trade, and industry compared to the Hindu community.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Mention any two ways in which the Treaty of Versailles affected the German Military Force.

questions.model_answer: Two ways the Treaty of Versailles affected the German military force were that its army was restricted to one lakh soldiers, and its navy was restricted to 15,000 men and only 24 ships, while its air force and submarines were banned altogether.

factual_anchors.context: Basis for peaceful co-existence in NAM

It chooses its own policy or way of life. Preserve the freedom of new nations from colonial influence and end imperialism./To protect human rights and environment/To condemn racial discrimination/To save the new nations from the supremacy of the superpowers/To eliminate nuclear weapons and ensure peaceful co-existence based on the Panchsheel Agreement/To abolish imperialism and promote freedom to pursue a free domestic and foreign policy./ To establish a new economic order./ To strengthen the UN./ To maintain International peace, harmony and/ Co-operation.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: From the passage, deduce and mention any two ways in which the Constitution ensures the independence of the Judiciary.

stimulus.text: When a judicial system is correctly calibrated, the law is applied by judges fearlessly, without favour or fear and with respect. That is why judicial security of tenure is so fundamental. It is also why judges must be properly paid without any interference from the Executive or Legislature.

key_points: Appointment of judges
Security of tenure or can work till 65 years of age
Salaries are charged on the Consolidated fund of India
No discussion with respect of the conduct of the Judges
Punishment for the contempt of Court
Prohibition of practice after retirement
Removal of Judges only through impeachment
Freedom to announce decisions and decrees without any fear
Salaries are not put to vote or cannot be changed to their disadvantage
Security must be provided to the Judges
Salaries of judges can be reduced only during a Financial Emergency
Has full control over its establishment or procedure of work

factual_anchors.context: Retirement age of judges ensuring security of tenure

questions.scheme_text: Appointment of judges. / Security of tenure or can work till 65 years of age. / Salaries are charged on the Consolidated fund of India / No discussion with respect of the conduct of the Judges / Punishment for the contempt of Court / Prohibition of practice after retirement / Removal of Judges only through impeachment./ Freedom to announce decisions and decrees without any fear / Salaries are not put to vote or cannot be changed to their disadvantage. / Security must be provided to the Judges./ Salaries of judges can be reduced only during a Financial Emergency/ has full control over its establishment or procedure of work. (Any two)
questions.model_answer: Two ways the Constitution ensures the independence of the Judiciary, as can be deduced from the passage, are the security of tenure given to judges, so that they can work without fear, and the charging of their salaries on the Consolidated Fund of India, so that these cannot be reduced to their disadvantage or made subject to a vote.
questions.examiner_comment: Several candidates were able to deduce the answer correctly and could identify the key words from the passage.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Provide exposure to students of varied relevant passages from newspapers and books for strengthening comprehension skills.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Parliament of India comprises the President and the two houses. With reference to the Indian Parliament, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three circumstances under which the Parliament can make laws on subjects in the state list.
key_points: During an emergency
When approved by 2/3 majority by the Rajya Sabha
When two or more states ask
When the state is under President's Rule or Emergency due to breakdown of constitutional Machinery

factual_anchors.context: Majority required by Rajya Sabha to authorize Parliament to legislate on State List

questions.scheme_text: During an emergency/when approved by 2/3 majority by the Rajya Sabha/When two or more states ask./ When the state is under President's Rule or Emergency due to breakdown of constitutional Machinery. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Parliament can make laws on subjects in the State List during a national emergency, when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by a two-thirds majority authorising it to do so, and when two or more states themselves request Parliament to legislate on a State subject.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates answered this question correctly. In general, candidates demonstrated a clear understanding of the concept of Parliament making laws on subjects in the State List. However, a few candidates could not provide a complete response and mentioned only one or two correct points. A number of candidates explained the term adequately. At the same time, the same number of candidates appeared unfamiliar with the concept altogether and showed confusion regarding the exclusive powers of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the powers of the Parliament with relevant examples. Moreover, discuss the unitary features of the Indian Constitution, even though India has a federal structure. Prepare a classification chart to give students a clear overview of the key differences between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, with particular focus on their respective powers.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Parliament of India comprises the President and the two houses. With reference to the Indian Parliament, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Explain the following terms: (a) Question Hour (b) Quorum (c) No Confidence Motion
key_points: Question hour: The (first) hour or 11 a.m. of the house when questions are asked by the members / questions asked to obtain or seek information on matters of public importance / the right to interpellation in the house / Types of questions / a 10 day notice is given to ask questions
Quorum: Minimum number of members required to be present in order to enable the house to transact business / 1/10 or 10% of the total membership of each house

No-Confidence Motion: Moved by the opposition / If it is passed the Government falls / motion to express lack of confidence in the Government / It passed, the whole ministry has to resign / A motion can be moved only in the LS / A motion used by the LS to control the executive / 50 members need to support its introduction

factual_anchors.context: Quorum requirement — 10% of total membership
Members needed to support introduction of No-Confidence Motion
Days notice for asking questions in Question Hour

questions.scheme_text:
(a) Question hour: The (first) hour or 11 a.m. of the house when questions are asked by the members./questions asked to obtain or seek information on matters of public importance/the right to interpellation in the house./ Types of questions/ a 10 day notice is given to ask questions. (Any one)
(b) Quorum: Minimum number of members required to be present in order to enable the house to transact business / 1/10 or 10% of the total membership of each house. (Any one)
(c) No-Confidence Motion: Moved by the opposition / If it is passed the Government falls./ motion to express lack of confidence in the Government./It passed, the whole ministry has to resign./A motion can be moved only in the LS./A motion used by the LS to control the executive. / 50 members need to support its introduction. (Any one)
questions.model_answer: Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting, usually at 11 a.m., when members ask questions to seek information on matters of public importance. Quorum is the minimum number of members — one-tenth of the total membership of the House — who must be present to enable it to transact business. A No-Confidence Motion is a motion moved by the opposition, only in the Lok Sabha, expressing a lack of confidence in the government; if passed, the entire Council of Ministers is bound to resign.
questions.examiner_comment: The question was attempted well by most candidates, although some were unable to answer all three subparts accurately. Of the three components, the majority responded correctly to questions on 'Question Hour' and 'Quorum'. However, a few candidates displayed uncertainty and confusion in explaining the concept and implications of a 'No Confidence Motion'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the parliamentary procedures and related terms with relevant examples to avoid confusion. Use real-life examples or case studies to illustrate each procedure. By providing a comprehensive understanding of these procedures and addressing common misconceptions, students will develop a more nuanced and accurate perspective on parliamentary functioning.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Parliament of India comprises the President and the two houses. With reference to the Indian Parliament, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: When can the term of the Lok Sabha be extended? Mention any three powers of the Lok Sabha which show its superiority over the Rajya Sabha.
key_points: During an emergency
Motion of No-Confidence against the government can only be introduced or passed in the Lok Sabha
The Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha only
Money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha
Budget is passed / or monetary controls the national purse / has complete control over finance
In case of a deadlock between the two houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails due to its higher numerical strength
Can pass an Adjournment Motion
Has a greater say in the election of the President & VC
Can pass supplementary grants
Vote on account
Directly elected by the People
Passing of grants
Cut motion
Increase or decrease of tax
Censure motion
questions.scheme_text:
During an emergency
Lok Sabha-Motion of No-Confidence against the government can only be introduced or passed in the Lok Sabha. / the Council of Ministers is answerable to the Lok Sabha only. / Money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. / Budget is passed./ or monetary controls the national purse/has complete control over finance. / In case of a deadlock between the two houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails due to its higher numerical strength. / Can pass an Adjournment Motion./ has a greater say in the election of the President & VC./ Can pass supplementary grants./ Vote on account./ Directly elected by the People./ Passing of grants./ Cut motion./ Increase or decrease of tax./ Censure motion. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: The term of the Lok Sabha can be extended during a national emergency. Three powers that show its superiority over the Rajya Sabha are that a Motion of No-Confidence can only be introduced and passed in the Lok Sabha; Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, giving it complete control over the national purse; and in case of a deadlock between the two Houses, the will of the Lok Sabha prevails because of its greater numerical strength.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by majority of the candidates; however, some candidates could not answer the first part of the question about the extension of the term of the Lok Sabha, correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Prepare a classification chart to help students understand the differences in the qualifications, term, composition, and functions of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Explain the exclusive powers of both Houses with examples and present them in a tabular format for easier recall. Highlight the specific roles of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha within the Indian Parliamentary system.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the country is vested in the President and Vice President. With reference to this answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Explain the impeachment process through which the Parliament can remove the President from power.
key_points: On grounds of the violation of Constitution or misbehaviour or incapacity
Motion is introduced in either house
14 day notice in writing
Notice by 1/4 of the total number of members in the house
It has to be passed by the 2/3 majority in the house it is introduced
The first house frames charges
The other house investigates
The President or his representative can be present
If 2/3 majority agrees to the motion, it is passed
If any one house disagrees, the motion is dropped
There will be no joint session
Both houses have to pass the motion

factual_anchors.context: Members needed to initiate impeachment notice
Majority needed to pass the impeachment motion
Days notice in writing required

questions.scheme_text: On grounds of the violation of Constitution or misbehaviour or incapacity. / Motion is introduced in either house. / 14 day notice in writing. / Notice by 1/4 of the total number of members in the house. / It has to be passed by the 2/3 majority in the house it is introduced. / the first house frames charges./The other house investigates. / The President or his representative can be present / If 2/3 majority agrees to the motion, it is passed / If any one house disagrees, the motion is dropped./ there will be no joint session./ Both houses have to pass the motion. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: The President can be impeached on the ground of violating the Constitution. The charge is introduced as a motion in either House, after a 14-day written notice signed by at least one-fourth of that House's members. The House in which the motion originates frames the charge, which the other House investigates; if it is passed by a two-thirds majority in both Houses separately, the President stands removed from office.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates; however, some candidates did not follow the correct order of the impeachment procedure. A few candidates were not familiar with the concept of the impeachment process.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the concept of impeachment using a flow chart to ensure students know the steps involved in impeachment in the sequential manner. Explain that impeachment is a process intended to remove the President for a 'violation of the Constitution'. Emphasise that impeachment is not the result of political disagreements but requires proven constitutional violations. Use a flowchart or visual timeline to simplify the steps for students.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the country is vested in the President and Vice President. With reference to this answer the following questions:

key_points: Maintains order in the house
Can suspend an unruly member
Can adjourn the house in case of grave disorder
Can expunge unparliamentary words
Decides if there is a contempt of House
Regulates debates and proceedings
Presides over the meetings
Admissibility of questions and resolutions
All bills passed in the house are authenticated by him
Casting vote or explanation of the casting vote
Interprets rules / Decision of the Chairman is final
Ex-officio Chairman of Committees
Appoints Chairpersons of Committees
If a secret document has to be brought up, it is only done so with the permission of the Chairman
Chairman communicates all decisions of the house to concerned authorities
Allows admissibility of strangers and press
Presides over conferences of presiding officers of Legislative bodies
Conducts the business of RS
Delegates are sent to foreign countries by consulting the Chairman
Can disqualify members under anti-defection law
questions.scheme_text: Maintains order in the house./Can suspend an unruly member./Can adjourn the house in case of grave disorder. /Can expunge unparliamentary words. /Decides if there is a contempt of House. / Regulates debates and proceedings. / Presides over the meetings. / Admissibility of questions and resolutions. / All bills passed in the house are authenticated by him. / Casting vote or explanation of the casting vote. / Interprets rules / Decision of the Chairman is final. / Ex-officio Chairman of Committees. / Appoints Chairpersons of Committees. / If a secret document has to be brought up, it is only done so with the permission of the Chairman. / Chairman communicates all decisions of the house to concerned authorities / Allows admissibility of strangers and press. / Presides over conferences of presiding officers of Legislative bodies./ Conducts the business of RS./ delegates are sent to foreign countries by consulting the Chairman./ Can disqualify members under anti-defection law. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three powers of the Vice President as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are that he maintains order in the House and can suspend an unruly member; he decides all questions of procedure, since his decision on the rules is final; and he presides over the meetings of the House, authenticating all bills passed by it.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered this question well. However, some candidates were confused and mentioned the functions of the Vice President, while the question specified the latter's powers as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the dual role played by the Vice President with examples to help the students distinguish between these two roles — one as the Vice President and the other as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Parallels can be drawn between the functions of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the functions of the Rajya Sabha Chairman, for building conceptual clarity.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Executive Power of the country is vested in the President and Vice President. With reference to this answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: With reference to the powers of President, mention: (a) Any two Financial Powers (b) Any two Executive Powers
key_points: Financial powers: A money bill cannot be introduced except on the recommendation of the President
Financial powers: Budget
Financial powers: Contingency funds
Financial powers: Annual financial statement
Financial powers: Appoints finance commission which makes recommendation to the President
Financial powers: Controls the consolidated Fund of India
Executive powers: Head of the Indian Union
Executive powers: Formation of the Council of Ministers
Executive powers: Power to appoint and remove high officials or dignitaries of State
Executive powers: The administration of Union Territories
Executive powers: Control over State Governments

Executive powers: Appointment of Governors / Judges / Attorney General / Chairman of Planning Commission / Comptroller Auditor General / Public Service Commission / Prime Minister / Ambassadors and Diplomats / Chief Election Commissioner / Lt. Governors or Chief Commissioners / Members of the Finance Commission
Executive powers: All executive orders are issued in his/her name
questions.scheme_text:
(a) Financial powers: A money bill cannot be introduced except on the recommendation of the President. / Budget / Contingency funds / Annual financial statement / Appoints finance commission which makes recommendation to the President./ Controls the consolidated Fund of India. (Any two)
(b) Executive powers: Head of the Indian Union / Formation of the Council of Ministers / Power to appoint and remove high officials or dignitaries of State. / The administration of Union Territories / Control over State Governments / Appointment of Governors / Judges / Attorney General / Chairman of Planning Commission / Comptroller Auditor General / Public Service Commission / Prime Minister. / Ambassadors and Diplomats./ Chief Election Commissioner./ Lt. Governors. Or Chief Commissioners. / Members of the Finance Commission./ All executive orders are issued in his/her name. (Any two)
questions.model_answer: Two financial powers of the President are that a Money Bill cannot be introduced in Parliament except on his recommendation, and that the Budget is presented to Parliament in his name. Two executive powers of the President are that he is the head of the Indian Union in whose name all executive orders are issued, and that he appoints the Governors of States as well as the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
questions.examiner_comment: (a) This question was well attempted by most of the candidates. (b) Majority of the candidates answered this question appropriately, while some candidates mixed it up with Legislative functions.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Elucidate the difference between the various powers of the President. Clear the demarcation for the candidates. Explain with examples the meaning of the words Financial, Legislative, and Executive powers with reference to the President for better understanding. Discuss in class that Executive powers denote appointments and legislative powers are connected to Parliamentary functions.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The High Courts of India are the highest courts of appeal in each state. With reference to the High Courts of India, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: What is meant by the term Original Jurisdiction of the High Court? Mention any two cases which fall under this jurisdiction.
key_points: Original Jurisdiction: Extends to those cases which the High Court has authority to hear and decide in the first instance / Cases which come directly to High Court
Cases: Wills
Divorce
Marriage
Company law
Admiralty
Contempt of Court
Constitutional cases
Interprets the Constitution
Enforcement of Fundamental Rights or Issue of writs
Election petition
State revenue and its collection
Judicial review
questions.scheme_text:
Original Jurisdiction: Extends to those cases which the High Court has authority to hear and decide in the first instance./ Cases which come directly to High Court.
Cases: Wills / Divorce / Marriage / Company law / Admiralty / Contempt of Court / Constitutional cases / Interprets the Constitution / Enforcement of Fundamental Rights or Issue of writs / Election petition / State revenue and its collection / Judicial review. (Any two)
questions.model_answer: Original Jurisdiction refers to those cases which the High Court has the authority to hear and decide in the first instance, rather than on appeal. Two cases that fall under this jurisdiction are matters relating to wills, divorce, and marriage, and cases involving the enforcement of Fundamental Rights through the issue of writs.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered this question correctly. However, some candidates were found to be confused between the High Court and the Supreme Court cases. The common error made by a large number of candidates was that they mentioned 'all civil cases' and 'all criminal cases' instead of specific examples of cases that are a part of the 'Original Jurisdiction of High Court'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the meaning of the Original Jurisdiction with relevant examples. Encourage students to make a comparative table of cases to distinguish between 'the Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court' and 'the High Court'. Guide students to mention specific examples of 'the types of cases' instead of 'general terms'.
questions.common_error: Mentioning 'all civil cases' and 'all criminal cases' instead of specific examples

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The High Courts of India are the highest courts of appeal in each state. With reference to the High Courts of India, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any two advantages of the Lok Adalat. Mention any one difference between the Sessions Court and the Court of the District Judge.
key_points: Spirit of compromise
Delivers speedy / fast or quick justice or Saves time
Inexpensive justice or cheap / economical / no court fee / the fee will be refunded if case is settled
Awards passed by Lok Adalats are final and binding, or No appeal in any court against decision
Reduce the workload of subordinate or other Courts or reduces backlog
Can pass awards at a pre-litigation stage
Promotes social justice
Settlement of families' disputes or between neighbours
Minor cases of assault / no ill feeling / can move the application on a plain paper
No need of lawyers
Free legal aid to weaker sections
People's court which can be arranged anywhere
Session Courts: Highest Criminal Court of the district / Presides by session Judge

Court of the District Judge: Highest Civil Court of the district / Presides by the District Judge / District Judge acts as the Deputy Commissioner and District Collector / Session Judge does not perform administrative functions
questions.scheme_text:
Spirit of compromise. / Delivers speedy speedy fast or quick justice or Saves time. /inexpensive justice or cheap/economical./no court fee/ the fee will be refunded if case is settled / Awards passed by Lok Adalats are final and binding, or No appeal in any court against decision. / Reduce the workload of subordinate or other Courts or reduces backlog. / Can pass awards at a pre-litigation stage. / Promotes social justice. / Settlement of families' disputes or between neighbours. / Minor cases of assault./no ill feeling/can move the application on a plain paper./ No need of lawyers./ Free legal aid to weaker sections./ People's court which can be arranged anywhere.
Session Courts: Highest Criminal Court of the district./ Presides by session Judge.
Court of the District Judge: Highest Civil Court of the district./ Presides by the District Judge./ District Judge acts as the Deputy Commissioner and District Collector./ Session Judge does not perform administrative functions.
questions.model_answer: Two advantages of the Lok Adalat are that it settles disputes in the spirit of compromise, delivering speedy and inexpensive justice with no court fee, and that its awards are final and binding, with no appeal lying against them in any court. One difference between the two courts is that the Sessions Court is the highest criminal court of the district, while the Court of the District Judge is the highest civil court of the district.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was answered correctly by most of the candidates, but a few candidates wrote about village panchayats. In the second sub-part, majority of the candidates wrote appropriate answers; however, the difference between 'the Sessions Court' and 'the Court of the District Judge' was not understood by some of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Focus on the topics namely 'definition of Lok Adalats' as a 'Court of People' and its advantages. Also, deliberate in class the 'advantages of the Lok Adalat' with some examples. Explain the difference between the 'Sessions Court' and 'the Court of the District Judge' with examples for better understanding. Guide students to write examples correctly to build conceptual clarity.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The High Courts of India are the highest courts of appeal in each state. With reference to the High Courts of India, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Explain the following with reference to the High Court: (a) Revisory Jurisdiction (b) Court of Record
key_points: Revisory Jurisdiction: Subordinate Court has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it
High Court may call for a record of any case heard by the subordinate court if an injustice or an error has happened
Violation of the principles of natural justice
Arbitrary decision leading to wrong judgement
Error in procedure
Sets aside the subordinate court's verdict if in error and announces a new judgement
Miscarriage of Judgement
Court of Record: Its judgments and orders are preserved as a record
This can be produced in any court as precedents / future references / testimony
If a person commits a contempt of court, the court has the authority to punish her/him for contempt
No authorities can deprive the court of this right
It is not applicable to other high courts
Subordinate courts have to follow the high courts of their respective statements while giving judgements in similar cases
questions.scheme_text:
(a) Revisory Jurisdiction: Subordinate Court has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it. / High Court may call for a record of any case heard by the subordinate court if an injustice or an error has happened. / Violation of the principles of natural justice. / Arbitrary decision leading to wrong judgement. / Error in procedure. / Sets aside the subordinate court's verdict if in error and announces a new judgement./ Miscarriage of Judgement. (Any two)
(b) The court of record. Its judgments and orders are preserved as a record/ This can be produced in any court as precedents/.future references/testimony/ If a person commits a contempt of court, the court has the authority to punish her/him for contempt. /No authorities can deprive the court of this right / It is not applicable to other high courts./ Subordinate courts have to follow the high courts of their respective statements while giving judgements in similar cases. (Any two)
questions.model_answer: Revisory Jurisdiction allows the High Court to call for the record of any case decided by a subordinate court if it has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it, or if an injustice or error has occurred, and to set aside that court's verdict and pass a fresh judgement. The Court of Record means the High Court's judgements and orders are preserved as a record that can be produced in any court as a precedent, and that it has the authority to punish anyone who commits contempt of court.
questions.examiner_comment: (a) Several candidates were confused between 'the Revisory Jurisdiction' and 'Judicial Review'. The remaining candidates were confused between the 'Revisory Jurisdiction of the High Court' and 'the Supreme Court'. (b) This question was well attempted by a large number of candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the meaning of the term and the 'jurisdictions of the High Court' thoroughly to students with relevant examples from newspaper reports to avoid confusion between these two concepts i.e. 'Revisory Jurisdiction of the High Court' and 'the Supreme Court'. Provide a comparative table of the Jurisdictions of the High Courts and the Supreme Court for better clarity. Discuss and reiterate the Court of Record with valid points like those whose proceedings and judgements are recorded and preserved as evidence for future reference, testimony, and enforcing the legal rights based on established precedents.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Revolt of 1857 was conscious beginning of the independence struggle against the British. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: What was the Doctrine of Lapse? Who introduced it?
key_points: Doctrine of Lapse: The policy of expansion
Where if a king did not have a natural heir
The kingdom would lapse to the British
The adopted son would not be allowed to rule
Rulers had to take the permission of the British to adopt
Lord Dalhousie

factual_anchors.context: Introduced the Doctrine of Lapse

questions.scheme_text:
Doctrine of Lapse: The policy of expansion / where if a king did not have a natural heir / the kingdom would lapse to the British / the adopted son would not be allowed to rule./ Rulers had to take the permission of the British to adopt. (Any two)
Lord Dalhousie
questions.model_answer: The Doctrine of Lapse was a policy of expansion under which, if a ruler died without a natural heir, his kingdom would lapse to the British; an adopted son was not allowed to succeed to the throne unless the British had earlier sanctioned the adoption. It was introduced by Lord Dalhousie.
questions.examiner_comment: A large number of candidates could describe the Doctrine of Lapse correctly; however, some candidates were not able to mention the person who introduced the policy.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Present all the repressive policies in a tabular form to avoid confusion. Explain the Governor-Generals, their influences, and their impacts using a timeline. Use a flowchart to depict the various policies introduced by different Governor-Generals to help students understand them better.

questions.subject: history_civics

(Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three socio-religious causes of the Revolt of 1857 were the British policy of interfering with the social customs of Indians, apprehensions about Western innovations such as the introduction of railways and telegraph, and fears among the people, encouraged by the activities of Christian missionaries, of mass conversion to Christianity.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates, as most of the candidates were able to accurately identify and explain the key features of the socio-religious causes that contributed to the First War of Independence. However, a few candidates could not give complete details of the question asked.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Use mind maps and other graphic organisers for better clarity and segregation while teaching the causes. Elucidate the policies with examples of Indians affected. Incorporate videos and role plays in class to make the topic more engaging. Draw parallels between society in 1857 and that of today to make the topic more relatable for students.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Revolt of 1857 was conscious beginning of the independence struggle against the British. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any four military causes which led to this Revolt.
key_points: Ill treatment of Indian soldiers

Bhatta Deprivation of Allowances
Faulty distribution of troops

Discontent or disaffection in the Bengal Army
Introduction of Enfield rifles or incident of greased cartridges
Soldiers were ill-fed / badly housed / poorly paid or less salaries

Main source of disaffection

questions.scheme_text: Ill treatment of Indian soldiers. / General Service Enlistment Act. / Larger Proportion of Indians in the British army. / Bleak prospects of promotions. / Bhatta Deprivation of Allowances. / Faulty distribution of troops. / Poor performance of British troops or loss of prestige in Afghan war. / Discontent or disaffection in the Bengal Army. / Introduction of Enfield rifles or incident of greased cartridges./ Soldiers were ill-fed./ badly housed./ poorly paid or less salaries./ Soldiers were not allowed to wear caste or sect marks./ Free postage was cancelled./ Unemployment caused by the disbanding of armies. (Any four)
questions.model_answer: Four military causes of the Revolt were the ill-treatment of Indian soldiers and the larger proportion of Indians relative to Europeans in the army; the General Service Enlistment Act, which threatened to send sepoys overseas against their religious beliefs; discontent in the Bengal Army over bleak prospects of promotion; and the introduction of the Enfield rifle, whose greased cartridges were rumoured to be coated with cow and pig fat.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the causes of the Revolt of 1857 under subheadings such as Economic Causes, Military Causes, and Political Causes to avoid overlapping. Presenting them in a tabular form will help students gain better clarity.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The oppressive British colonial rule led to the growth of nationalism in India. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: The repressive policies of Lord Lytton became a catalyst to the growth of nationalism. Mention any three of his repressive policies to justify this statement.
key_points: Removed import duties on cotton textiles
He reduced the age for appearing in the Indian Civil Service Examination (from 21 to 19)
Indian Arms Act
Vernacular Press Act
Organised the grand Delhi Darbar when India was facing famine

factual_anchors.context: Repressive policy restricting Indian press
Prohibited Indians from possessing arms
Reduced ICS exam age from 21 to 19

questions.scheme_text: Removed import duties on cotton textiles / He reduced the age for appearing in the Indian Civil Service Examination (from 21 to 19) / Indian Arms Act / Vernacular Press Act / Organised the grand Delhi Darbar when India was facing famine. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three repressive policies of Lord Lytton were the Vernacular Press Act, which curbed the freedom of the Indian language press; the Indian Arms Act, which restricted Indians from possessing arms; and lowering the age limit for the Indian Civil Service examination from twenty-one to nineteen, which made it harder for Indians to qualify.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates. However, a few candidates mistakenly included 'Ilbert Bill' as a 'policy of Lord Lytton'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Provide a clear historical context for the Grand Delhi Darbar and other policies, explaining their significance and purpose. Make a clear distinction between the repressive policies of Lord Lytton and the positive reforms by Sir Ilbert. Explain the power of Viceroys in their colonial actions, and policies in detail for better clarity.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The oppressive British colonial rule led to the growth of nationalism in India. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three ways in which the Press promoted nationalism.
key_points: Developing Nationalism
Keeping people informed of the political developments

Modern liberal ideals of liberty, freedom, equality, home rule and independence spread
Patriotism
Daily criticism of the unjust policies of the British Government in India

Development of National literature
Exchange of views
Awareness to understand the political and social development of the outside world
To shape their policies and programmes
Spreading message of Natural Rights

Names of newspapers and books
questions.scheme_text: Developing Nationalism. / Keeping people informed of the political developments. / Journals and papers gave a national character. / Struggle against press censorship. / Modern liberal ideals of liberty, freedom, equality, home rule and independence spread. / Patriotism / Daily criticism of the unjust policies of the British Government in India. / Exposed the true nature of the British rule in India. / Development of National literature. / Exchange of views. / Awareness to understand the political and social development of the outside world. / To shape their policies and programme.s / Spreading message of Natural Rights./ Brought the leaders and the workers on a common platform./ Helped in organising political movements./ Names of newspapers and books. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three ways the Press promoted nationalism were by keeping people informed of political developments and giving them a national character, by daily criticising the unjust policies of the British Government in India, and by spreading modern liberal ideals of liberty, freedom, and self-rule, which brought leaders and ordinary people onto a common platform.
questions.examiner_comment: A large number of candidates attempted this part correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Illustrate the role of the Press by showing students various reports of the freedom movement reported by the newspapers during the period from 1857 to 1947. Discuss the role of the press in the Indian national movement to help students understand the way ideas sparked revolutions, and the way words became weapons against colonialism.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The oppressive British colonial rule led to the growth of nationalism in India. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Who presided over the second session of the Indian National Congress? Mention any three objectives of the Congress.
key_points: Dadabhai Naoroji
To enable the national workers from all parts of India personally known to each other
To end all racial, religious and provincial prejudices
To train and organise public opinion in the country
To promote friendly relations between Nationalist Political workers from the different parts of the country

Decide upon political tasks or jobs to be undertaken during the year

factual_anchors.context: Presided over the second session of the Indian National Congress

questions.scheme_text:
Dadabhai Naoroji
To enable the national workers from all parts of India personally known to each other. / To end all racial, religious and provincial prejudices. / To train and organise public opinion in the country. / To promote friendly relations between Nationalist Political workers from the different parts of the country. / To develop the feeling of national unity. / To formulate popular demands and present them to the Government. / Decide upon political tasks or jobs to be undertaken during the year. questions.model_answer: Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the second session of the Indian National Congress. questions.teacher_suggestion: Define the objectives of the various parties and organisations with examples to avoid confusion. Provide a stimulus related to the second session of the INC and derive objectives from the information provided in the case studies.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.period: Mass Phase of the National Movement (1915-1947)
questions.parent_question_text: Look at the given picture and answer the questions that follows:
questions.question_text: Mention any three repressive provisions of the Rowlatt Act.
key_points: The public and newspaper men not allowed to attend the trial or In-camera trial
No appeal against judgement
Search any place
Arrest anyone without giving any reason or warrant
Restriction on movement of individuals
Suspension of the Right of Habeas Corpus
No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal

factual_anchors.context: Repressive act of 1919

questions.scheme_text: The public and newspaper men not allowed to attend the trial or In-camera trial / No appeal against judgement. / Search any place. / Arrest anyone without giving any reason or warrant. / Restriction on movement of individuals. / Suspension of the Right of Habeas Corpus. / No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three repressive provisions of the Rowlatt Act were that a person could be arrested and imprisoned without a warrant or a stated reason; that the accused had no right of appeal against the judgement; and that the public and even the press were not allowed to attend the trial, which was held in-camera.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates attempted this part appropriately; however, some candidates could not write three repressive provisions of the Rowlatt Act.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Deliberate in class the way the Rowlatt Act severely curtailed civil liberties and led to widespread protests and opposition across India. Emphasise the reason for the Act and the way it was viewed as highly repressive and unjust by Indians. Teach the repressive policies of the Rowlatt Act effectively by making students feel the injustice, understand its impact, and see its historical importance.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.period: Mass Phase of the National Movement (1915-1947)
questions.parent_question_text: Look at the given picture and answer the questions that follows:
questions.question_text: Mention the following: (a) Any two causes of the Quit India Movement. (b) Any two causes of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
key_points: (a) Failure of the Cripps Mission
(a) Japanese Threat
(b) Simon Commission
(b) Declaration of Purna Swaraj
(b) Lahore session of Congress

factual_anchors.context: Its failure was a cause of the Quit India Movement
Cause of the Civil Disobedience Movement
Declaration of Purna Swaraj leading to CDM

questions.scheme_text:
(a) Failure of the Cripps Mission / Japanese Threat.
(b) Simon Commission / Declaration of Purna Swaraj/ Lahore session of Congress.
questions.model_answer: Two causes of the Quit India Movement were the failure of the Cripps Mission to satisfy Indian demands, and the threat of a Japanese invasion of India. Two causes of the Civil Disobedience Movement were the appointment of the all-White Simon Commission, and the declaration of Poorna Swaraj as the Congress's goal at its Lahore Session.
questions.examiner_comment: (a) Most candidates incorrectly answered this part as they did not have clarity on the exact causes. The candidates mentioned the events which led to the 'Movement' instead of 'causes of the Quit India Movement'. (b) A large number of candidates incorrectly included 'the Dandi March' and 'the Nehru Report' as causes of 'the Civil Disobedience Movement'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Specify two key causes of the Quit India Movement as per the scope of the syllabus. Adopt a structured approach by incorporating the historical context, highlighting major causes and events, and discussing the relevant objectives of related movements. Follow the Scope of syllabus to ensure students do not lose out marks due to confusion.

questions.subject: history_civics

stimulus.text: In an effort to secure resources for its expanding industries, Japan invaded the northern Chinese province of Manchuria. Although Western nations protested the Japanese action, most members of the League of Nations, including Canada, opposed any form of military intervention to defend Chinese sovereignty. A League of Nations commission, headed by the British diplomat Lord Lytton, was dispatched to Manchuria to investigate.

questions.parent_question_text: Read the passage given and answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: How did the incident being described above become a cause for the Second World War?
key_points: Japan was determined to dominate the Far East
Japan left the League
Japan attacked China
Invaded Manchuria / Occupied it / set up a government there
It started an undeclared war against China
China appealed to the League of Nations but Britain and France paid no attention to this appeal
Japan joined Germany and Italy to form the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo AXIS
Continued its policy of expansion and conquest
Japan left the League of Nations and started occupying British and American properties in China
France and Britain followed the policy of appeasement
They wanted Japan to be used to weaken China

factual_anchors.context: Region invaded by Japan
Alliance formed by Japan with Germany and Italy

questions.scheme_text: Japan was determined to dominate the Far East. / Japan left the League. / Japan attacked China. / Invaded Manchuria. / Occupied it. / set up a government there. It started an undeclared war against China. / China appealed to the League of Nations but Britain and France paid no attention to this appeal. / Japan joined Germany and Italy to form the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo AXIS./ continued its policy of expansion and conquest. / Japan left the League of Nations and started occupying British and American properties in China. / France, and Britain followed the policy of appeasement. / They wanted Japan to be used to weaken China. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Japan's invasion of Manchuria became a cause of the Second World War because Japan set up its own government there in defiance of China's sovereignty and then continued its policy of expansion and conquest; when China appealed to the League of Nations, Britain and France paid little attention, and Japan went on to leave the League altogether and later joined Germany and Italy to form the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo Axis.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates were able to answer this question correctly as the key words were evident in the passage. However, a few candidates copied the lines from the passage which lead to loss in marks.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Give students adequate practice in answering passage-based questions and discourage them from lifting answers directly from the passage. Train them to infer answers based on understanding rather than copying. Encourage reading of diverse passages related to historical events.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: Read the passage given and answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three reasons for Hitler's attack on Poland.
key_points: Hitler wanted to recapture the Port of Danzing which Germany had lost
He wanted to regain all territories they had lost due to the Treaty of Versailles
Germany had been divided into two to give Poland a land-route to the sea
Danzing was inhabited mainly by Germans
Germany could connect with East Prussia by occupying Danzing corridor
Germany signed a Non-Aggression Pact with Russia
Poland was accused of committing atrocities against Germans living there
Polish independence after World War I irked Germany

factual_anchors.context: Port city Germany wanted to recapture
Treaty that caused Germany's territorial losses
Pact signed with Russia before attacking Poland

questions.scheme_text: Hitler wanted to recapture the Port of Danzing which Germany had lost./He wanted to regain all territories they had lost due to the Treaty of Versailles./ Germany had been divided into two to give Poland a land-route to the sea./ Danzing was inhabited mainly by Germans. / Germany could connect with East Prussia by occupying Danzing corridor./ Germany signed a Non-Aggression Pact with Russia./ Poland was accused of committing atrocities against Germans living there./ Polish independence after World War I irked Germany. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three reasons for Hitler's attack on Poland were his wish to recapture the port of Danzig, which Germany had lost; his desire to regain all the territory Germany had lost under the Treaty of Versailles; and Germany's wish to reconnect with East Prussia by occupying the Polish or 'Danzig' Corridor, which had been created to give Poland access to the sea.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by most of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Draw students' attention to the importance of using precise points while answering instead of writing lengthy explanations for the reasons behind the attack. Discuss the context and consequences of Hitler's actions, helping students develop a comprehensive understanding of how these events led to the outbreak of war.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: Read the passage given and answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any four reasons for the failure of the League of Nations.
key_points: USA did not join the League and countries which joined were not interested in collective security
It was unable to stop the rise of dictatorship
League was helpless when France attacked Lithuania
Japan seized Manchuria
Italy attacked Ethiopia and Hitler attacked Czechoslovakia and annexed Austria
In every crisis, the countries either defied or ignored the League
It did not have an army of its own
An economic sanction against aggressor nation was of no use as the member states were not willing to apply the sanctions which affected the economy
Countries lost faith in the League
Countries entered into mutual political and military alliances
Policy of appeasement
Germany was not allowed to be the member
Russia was not part of the League
Failed to maintain Peace or could not stop the world war
Could not stop acts of aggression by France and Italy

factual_anchors.context: Did not join the League of Nations
League failed to prevent aggression
League failed to prevent aggression

questions.scheme_text: USA did not join the League and/ countries which joined were not interested in collective security. / It was unable to stop the rise of dictatorship. / League was helpless when France attacked Lithuania. / Japan seized Manchuria. / Italy attacked Ethiopia and Hitler attacked Czechoslovakia and annexed Austria. / In every crisis, the countries either defied or ignored the League. / It did not have an army of its own. / An economic sanction against aggressor nation was of no use as the member states were not willing to apply the sanctions which affected the economy. / Countries lost faith in the League. / Countries entered into mutual political and military alliances./ Policy of appeasement./ Germany was not allowed to be the member./ Russia was not part of the League./ Failed to maintain Peace or could not stop the world war./ Could not stop acts of aggression by France and Italy. (Any four)
questions.model_answer: Four reasons for the failure of the League of Nations were that the USA never joined it, weakening its authority from the start; it had no army of its own with which to enforce its decisions; economic sanctions against aggressor states proved useless since member states were unwilling to apply them at cost to their own economies; and it stood helpless as Japan seized Manchuria and Italy attacked Ethiopia.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of candidates could answer this question correctly, while some candidates wrote 'generalised answers' instead of 'specific points to explain the failure of the League of Nations'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Encourage students to cite specific instances and reasons for failures, and avoid generalised responses. Discuss the League of Nations with reference to its formation, objectives, and failure to prevent aggression by rising powers such as Germany and Japan. Link it to the Second World War by explaining how the League's inefficacy and the breakdown of peace efforts contributed to the rise of totalitarian regimes.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The organs and the agencies of the United Nation Organisation work towards the development of the world. With reference to this answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: What is the composition of the General Assembly?
key_points: All members of the United Nations are members of the General Assembly
Each state has five representatives in the General Assembly
Each state has only one vote
It is a Parliament of Nations
Assembly elects a new President
21 Vice Presidents
Chairman of six main committees
The Presidency rotates each year among five groups of states
Decisions are taken by 2/3 majority
The members meet once in a year
Special sessions can be called

factual_anchors.context: Representatives per state in the General Assembly
Number of Vice Presidents
Majority required for decisions

questions.scheme_text:
Composition of General Assembly
- All members of the United Nations are members of the General Assembly.
- Each state has five representatives in the General Assembly.
- Each state has only one vote.
- It is a Parliament of Nations.
- Assembly elects a new President.
- 21 Vice Presidents.
- Chairman of six main committees.
- The Presidency rotates each year among five groups of states.
- Decisions are taken by 2/3 majority.
- The members meet once in a year.
- Special sessions can be called. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: The General Assembly is composed of all member states of the United Nations, each of which may send up to five representatives but has only one vote. It is often called the 'Parliament of Nations,' and it elects a new President each year, with the Presidency rotating among five groups of states.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by most of the candidates, but some candidates were confused between 'the composition of the Security Council' and 'the General Assembly'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: For the conceptual clarity of the students, train them to prepare a chart reflecting comparative differences between the composition of the General Assembly, Security Council, and International Court of Justice.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The organs and the agencies of the United Nation Organisation work towards the development of the world. With reference to this answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three functions of the International Court of Justice.
key_points: Advisory opinion on legal matters to the organs of special agencies of the UN
Decides disputes between member states when referred
Disputes concerning interpretation of international law
Decides the compensation to be paid in case of breach of contract
Codification of International Law
Disputes regarding treaties signed between countries
Peaceful settlements of Disputes
Decides cases based on International Law
Legal advice is available only for member states
questions.scheme_text:
Three functions of the International Court of Justice:
- Advisory opinion on legal matters to the organs of special agencies of the UN.
- Decides disputes between member states when referred.
- Disputes concerning interpretation of international law.
- Decides the compensation to be paid in case of breach of contract.
- Codification of International Law.
- Disputes regarding treaties signed between countries.
- Peaceful settlements of Disputes.
- Decides cases based on International Law.
- Legal advice is available only for member states. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: Three functions of the International Court of Justice are to decide disputes between member states when a dispute is referred to it, to give advisory opinions on legal matters to the organs and special agencies of the UN, and to settle disputes concerning the interpretation of international law and treaties.
questions.examiner_comment: A large number of candidates were confused and could not mention three functions. Some candidates mentioned incomplete headings like Voluntary Jurisdiction, etc. without specifying the exact functions.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Train students to learn the functions in simple points instead of long explanations. Guide students to frame responses with complete and specific headings.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The organs and the agencies of the United Nation Organisation work towards the development of the world. With reference to this answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Give the full form of UNICEF. Mention any three of its functions.
key_points: UNICEF – United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund or United Nations Children's Fund
Works for protection of children / survival of children / health and well being
Provides funds for training personnel / health and sanitation workers / teachers and nutritionists
Universal Child Immunisation against preventable diseases
Provides technical supplies / equipment and other aids / paper for textbooks / equipment and medicines to health clinics
Pipes and pumps to bring clean water to villages
Assists government to plan community based services / maternal and child health / nutrition / sanitation
Provides help to children and mothers in emergencies arising from natural calamities and epidemics
Makes effort to prevent diseases like Tuberculosis (TB) / malaria / eye diseases / skin diseases
Sole agency which speaks on behalf of children
Ensures children have access to education / clean water and toilets
Reduces infant mortality due to diarrhoea
Works to prevent iodine deficiency
Works for the rights of women
Reduces social inequalities based on gender, caste, ethnicity and region

factual_anchors.context: United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund

questions.scheme_text:
UNICEF – United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund
Or United Nations Children's Fund
Functions of the UNICEF:
Works for protection of children./survival of children/health and well being./provides funds for training personnel./health and sanitation workers/teachers and nutritionists/Universal Child Immunisation against preventable diseases./provides technical supplies./equipment and other aids/paper for textbooks /equipment and medicines to health clinics/pipes and pumps to bring clean water to villages/assists government to plan community based services/maternal and child health/nutrition/sanitation/provides help to children and mothers in emergencies arising from natural calamities and epidemics/makes effort to prevent diseases like Tuberculosis (TB)/malaria/eye diseases/skin diseases/sole agency which speaks on behalf of children/ensures children have access to education/clean water and toilets/reduces infant mortality due to diarrhoea./works to prevent iodine deficiency/works for the rights of women/ reduces social inequalities based on gender, caste, ethnicity and region. (Any three)
questions.model_answer: UNICEF stands for the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund, also known as the United Nations Children's Fund. Three of its functions are working for the protection, survival, and well-being of children; providing funds for training health and sanitation workers, teachers, and nutritionists; and ensuring children have access to education, clean water, and sanitation.
questions.examiner_comment: A large number of candidates attempted this question well. Most candidates wrote the functions correctly; however, a few were unable to write the full form of UNICEF correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Advise students to learn the expansion of acronyms with correct spellings.
